text: You've seen ordinary blocking throughout this chapter — one session waiting for another to finish. This lesson covers a more severe cousin of that: the deadlock.

Ordinary blocking resolves itself: the holder eventually commits or rolls back, and the waiter proceeds. A deadlock is different. It's a cycle — two or more transactions each waiting on a lock the other one holds — and neither side can ever resolve it alone.

Picture the classic case. Session A updates Product 680, holding that lock, then tries to update Product 681. Session B, meanwhile, already updated Product 681 and is holding that lock, then tries to update Product 680. Session A holds what B wants. Session B holds what A wants. Neither will release until it finishes, and neither can finish until it gets what the other is holding.

SQL Server doesn't let a cycle like that sit forever. A background process, the deadlock monitor, periodically checks the lock graph for exactly this pattern. When it finds one, it picks a deadlock victim, kills that transaction, and rolls it back — which releases its locks and lets the other transaction finally proceed.

The victim's session gets error 1205, telling it plainly that it was chosen as the deadlock victim and should rerun the transaction. The victim is generally whichever transaction is cheapest to roll back, not necessarily the one that caused the problem.

A busy, well-designed system can still hit this occasionally under concurrent load — it isn't automatically a sign of broken code. Next up: reading the actual deadlock graph SQL Server captures, to see exactly what happened.
